newsitem.title: DUBAI: Gulf Arabs to forge stand on U.S. attacks on Iraq.
newsitem.headline: Gulf Arabs to forge stand on U.S. attacks on Iraq.

text.p: Gulf Arab foreign ministers on Saturday faced the task of forging a united reaction to U.S. missile strikes on Iraq amid signs of differences in opinion.
The ministers of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) -- which groups U.S. allies Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman, Bahrain and the United Arab Emirates -- were due to meet in Riyadh.

The talks were scheduled before the missile strikes on Tuesday and Wednesday, prompted by the Iraqi army's intervention in northern Iraq to help a Kurdish faction seize a city from a rival group a week ago.

A statement by the GCC secretariat described the meeting as significant and said it would discuss latest developments in the north and south of Iraq, terrorism, relations with Iran and Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
"The meeting will be dominated by the U.S. attacks and how to come out with a united stand in light of the difference in opinions," one diplomat said.
Much of the Arab world has condemned the attacks as infringing on Iraq's sovereignty.

Of the six GCC states, who had all joined the U.S.-led multinational force that ended Iraq's 1990-91 occupation of Kuwait and supported further U.S. action against Iraqi President Saddam Hussein, only Kuwait has officially reacted to the missile strikes saying it fully understood the U.S. action.

"The opinion of some of the GCC states, especially the UAE and Qatar, is that Baghdad this time around did not threaten another country and was dealing with an internal problem. They see the U.S. attacks as unjustified," another diplomat said.

Gulf analysts say those opposed to the U.S. strikes might however stop short of openly criticising the United States, the only Western power they see capable of defending them in case of threats by their much larger neighbours, Iraq and Iran.
"Iraq is still the foe and the U.S. the ally...They would likely avoid condemning the U.S. action but at the same time stay clear from supporting it," one diplomat said.

Asked about the ministers' meeting, U.S. assistant secretary of state Robert Pelletreau said in an interview published by the London-based al-Hayat daily on Saturday: "I don't know what they will do...I think there is a general understanding of the motives behind our move (the missile attacks on Iraq)."
"I think there is comprehensive understanding that Saddam Hussein and the Iraqi regime continue to be a threat to security and stability in the Gulf," he said.
A Pentagon spokesman said on Friday the 44 cruise missiles fired by U.S. forces had severely damaged air defence facilities in southern Iraq.

Iraq asked the GCC members for support. "There will be a GCC meeting on Saturday. And from here I urge the brethren in the Arab Gulf to take in their meeting a stand in support of Iraq against the evil and infidel forces of America," senior foreign ministry undersecretary Saad al-Faisel said in an interview carried by Iraqi state-run television on Friday.
Diplomats doubted the ministers would meet Iraq's request.
Newspapers in Kuwait and Saudi Arabia blamed Baghdad for the tension, while those in the UAE and Qatar slammed the attacks. Diplomats said the split mirrored differences in official views.

"Maybe the foreign ministers of the Gulf Cooperation Council who will today discuss the issue of Iraq, will take the initiative of calling for preserving its (Iraq's) sovereignty and territorial unity," said the UAE's al-Bayan on Saturday.
